questions.q: In client-side discovery, which component picks the specific instance for a request?
options: A central hardware load balancer in front of the fleet
The DNS resolver, via round-robin records
The service registry itself, which proxies and forwards the call onward
The calling client, using instance data fetched from the registry

questions.q: How does server-side discovery route a request?
options: The client caches the entire instance list and rotates through it with local logic
The client calls a router or load balancer that queries the registry and forwards
The registry pushes each request to a chosen instance
A sidecar rewrites DNS answers inside the client pod

questions.q: Why do registries require heartbeats or health checks from instances?
options: So dead or unhealthy instances stop receiving traffic promptly
To measure per-instance latency percentiles for capacity dashboards
To authenticate services before they join the mesh
To decide which instance owns each data shard

questions.q: Which concern belongs in an API gateway rather than inside each microservice?
options: Validating the business rules of an order
Managing database transaction boundaries for every downstream write
Edge authentication, rate limiting, and request routing
Publishing domain events after state changes

questions.q: What is the main point of the Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) pattern?
options: Sharing one perfectly generic API across every client type the company supports
Giving each client type an API shaped to its specific needs
Caching frontend assets closer to users
Moving business logic into the CDN edge

questions.q: What is the main drawback of plain DNS for service discovery?
options: DNS cannot return more than one address per name
DNS requires TCP connections for every lookup
Internal hostnames leak to public resolvers by default
Cached TTLs delay clients noticing instance changes

questions.q: Which tool is purpose-built as a service registry with built-in health checking?
options: Kafka
Redis
Consul
Nginx

questions.q: In the self-registration pattern, which component writes the instance's address into the registry?
options: The service instance itself, on startup
The deployment orchestrator's control loop
The API gateway during its first probe
A registrar sidecar watching the container runtime for new workloads

questions.q: Your single API gateway saturates CPU at peak. Best structural fix?
options: Run several stateless gateway replicas behind a load balancer
Move authentication down into every backend service
Pin the heaviest clients to a dedicated gateway using sticky sessions
Scale the gateway vertically and cap client connections

questions.q: Instances sometimes crash without deregistering, and clients hit dead addresses briefly. What bounds this window?
options: Longer DNS TTLs so clients refresh less often
Client retry loops that keep attempting addresses until a healthy node answers
Heartbeat leases with TTL expiry evicting silent instances
Gateway-level caching of successful responses

questions.q: Compared with server-side discovery, what does client-side discovery mainly trade?
options: Registry consistency guarantees in exchange for a much simpler gateway tier
Security controls for raw connection speed
Fewer moving parts for higher latency
One less network hop against discovery logic duplicated in every client

questions.q: Every instance goes unhealthy simultaneously whenever the shared database blips, causing a full outage. Likely cause?
options: The heartbeat interval is far too long
Deep health checks include the shared DB, so one blip fails every instance at once
The registry lost quorum during the blip
The gateway's health probe timeout is shorter than the database's normal response time

questions.q: A service mesh sidecar primarily handles which traffic, versus an API gateway?
options: Client-to-edge traffic entering the platform
Outbound egress toward third-party internet APIs
Internal service-to-service (east-west) traffic
CDN origin-pull requests for static assets

questions.q: Where should per-customer API rate limits live so every backend is protected uniformly?
options: At the gateway, before requests fan out to services
In middleware replicated inside each service so limits sit closest to the work
In the database as row-level quotas
In the client SDK's request scheduler

questions.q: A mobile app issues six sequential API calls to render one screen over high-latency links. Standard fix?
options: Enable HTTP/2 so all six calls multiplex over a single connection
A BFF endpoint that aggregates the six calls into one response
Raise pagination sizes so each call returns more data
Cache all six responses on the device for reuse

questions.q: During a network partition, what does an AP registry like Eureka prefer to do?
options: Halt all discovery responses to preserve consistency
Elect a new leader before serving any reads
Aggressively evict every instance it cannot reach until the partition heals
Keep serving possibly stale instance lists so discovery still works

questions.q: Dozens of teams push routing and transformation logic into one shared gateway. What risk emerges?
options: TLS termination overhead grows quadratically
The gateway becomes a deploy bottleneck and shared blast radius for every team
Registry lookups begin timing out under the weight of accumulated configuration
East-west traffic bypasses the mesh entirely

questions.q: Rolling deploys cause brief 502s even though replacement instances pass health checks. What step is likely missing?
options: A startup health gate before new instances join the pool
A blue-green DNS swap between complete fleets instead of rolling replacement
Canary analysis on the first replica
Deregistering old instances and draining in-flight requests before stopping them

questions.q: Heartbeats arrive every 30s and eviction requires 3 consecutive misses. Roughly how long can a dead instance keep receiving traffic?
options: About 90 seconds of continued traffic
About 30 seconds of continued traffic
About 3 seconds of continued traffic
Until the next full deploy replaces the registry state

questions.q: The gateway authenticates users, then forwards the user ID in a plain header that services trust. Vulnerability?
options: Header size limits truncate long identifiers
Tokens replay across concurrent sessions
Anyone reaching a service directly can forge the header — sign it or isolate the network
Clock skew between gateway and services eventually invalidates every forwarded claim
